title: Git
text:
Introduction

This book is a Git tutorial for beginners. It shows you how to save the history of a project, how to share it on GitHub and how to work in a team with branches and pull requests.
If you get stuck while reading, ask the Git tutor chat. The next page has the link.

Basics (chapters 1 to 6): install Git, make commits, push and pull, and undo mistakes.
Teamwork (chapters 7 to 9): branches, merge conflicts, pull requests and issues.
Practice (chapter 10): exercises for pairs and a quiz to check what you learned.
Background (chapter 11): why Git works the way it does. This chapter is optional.

The commands are shown for the terminal. PowerShell on Windows works fine. Where it helps, the book also shows how to do the same in VS Code.

title: 1  Why version control?
text:
1.1 Important words
Imagine you work on a project with three team mates. Without a tool, you end up with files like project-final.zip, project-final-v2.zip and project-final-REALLY-final.zip. Nobody knows which version is the newest, and changes get lost.
Git solves this problem:
💡 Git and GitHub are not the same thing. Git is the program on your computer. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories.

title: 1  Why version control?
text:
Word
Meaning




Repository (repo)
A project folder that Git tracks. It contains all files and the complete history.


Commit
A saved snapshot of your project, with a message that describes the change.


Remote
A copy of the repository on a server, e.g. on GitHub. Its default name is origin.


Branch
A separate line of work. You can work on a branch without disturbing others.

title: 2  Setup
text:
2.1 Install Git
You only need to do this once on each computer.

title: 2  Setup
text:
Windows: download and install Git from https://git-scm.com. Keep the default settings.
Check that it works. Open a terminal (PowerShell or the terminal in VS Code) and type:

git --version

title: 2  Setup
text:
2.2 Tell Git who you are
Every commit stores your name and email address. Use the same email address as in your GitHub account, so GitHub can link your commits to you.
git config --global user.name "Max Mustermann"
git config --global user.email "max.mustermann@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

init.defaultBranch main: new repositories use main as the name of the first branch.
core.editor: when Git needs a message from you (e.g. for a merge commit, see chapter 7), it opens VS Code. Write or check the message, save and close the tab. Without this setting, Git opens the editor Vim in the terminal, which is hard to use for beginners.

💡 Stuck in Vim? Press Esc, type :wq and press Enter.

title: 2  Setup
text:
2.3 Sign in to GitHub

Create an account on https://github.com if you don’t have one.
The first time you push to GitHub (see chapter 4), a browser window opens and asks you to sign in. After that, Git remembers you.

💡 You cannot use your GitHub password directly in the terminal. Always sign in through the browser window.

title: 2  Setup
text:
2.4 VS Code
VS Code has Git built in. Open the Source Control view (the icon with the branches on the left side, or Ctrl+Shift+G). In this tutorial you learn the terminal commands, but you can do most steps in VS Code as well.

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.1 Get a repository
There are two ways to start:
a) Copy an existing repository from GitHub (this is what you do most of the time):
git clone downloads the complete repository including its history into a new folder.
b) Turn an existing folder into a new repository:
Both ways create a hidden folder called .git. This is where Git stores the history. You can see it with ls -Force (PowerShell) or ls -a (Git Bash).
💡 If there is no .git folder in your project, Git commands don’t work. Git will say fatal: not a git repository.
⚠️ Never delete or change the .git folder by hand. If you delete it, the whole history is gone.

title: 3  Your first repository
3  Your first repository
text:
3.2 The three areas

Git has three areas for your files:

Working directory: the files you see and edit in your folder.
Staging area: the changes you have chosen for your next commit.
Repository: all commits that are saved in the history.

So saving a change in Git is a two-step process: first you add the change to the staging area, then you commit it.
💡 A commit is saved only on your computer. Nobody else can see it until you push it (see chapter 4).

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.3 Check what has changed
Show which files are changed, new (untracked) or staged:
git status
Show the changed lines before you stage them:
git diff
Show the changed lines that are already staged:
git diff --staged
In VS Code, click on a file in the Source Control view to see the changes side by side.

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.4 Stage and commit
Add one file to the staging area:
git add <file>
Add all changed and new files to the staging area:
git add .
Save the staged changes as a new commit:
git commit -m "Add login form"
In VS Code: click + next to a file to stage it, write a message and click Commit.

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.5 Review before you commit
💡 We always review our changes during staging!
Don’t just type git add . without looking. Instead:

Look at each changed file with git diff or in VS Code.
Is the change correct and complete? Then stage it.
Stage all files that belong to one topic and commit them together.
Repeat with the next topic.

Example: you changed 27 files. 20 of them are for the new login page and 7 fix a bug in the menu. Make two commits, one for each topic.

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.6 Write good commit messages
A good commit message tells your team what changed. Your team mates should understand it without looking at the code.



❌ Bad
✅ Good




update
Add validation to registration form


fix
Fix crash when user list is empty


asdf
Remove unused images from pics folder


changes from Monday
Translate start page to English



Tips:

Start with a verb: Add, Fix, Remove, Change, Update.
Keep the first line short (about 50 characters).
If the commit belongs to a GitHub issue, add the issue number (see chapter 9).

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.7 Look at the history
git log --oneline
Each line is one commit: a short commit ID (e.g. 8756b24) and the message. Press q to leave the list.
To see the history of all branches as a graph:
git log --oneline --graph --all

title: 3  Your first repository
text:
3.8 Look at a commit
Every commit has an ID, e.g. 8756b24. Git also has short names for commits:

HEAD is the commit you are on right now (usually your newest commit).
HEAD~1 is one commit before HEAD, HEAD~2 is two commits before, and so on.

Show which lines a commit changed:
git show HEAD
git show 8756b24

title: 4  Working with a remote repository
text:
4.1 Push: send your commits to GitHub
Reference: https://medium.com/mindorks/what-is-git-commit-push-pull-log-aliases-fetch-config-clone-56bc52a3601c
Your commits are only on your computer. To share them, you use a remote repository, e.g. on GitHub.
When you push a new branch for the first time, you have to tell Git where to send it:
After that, git push is enough. In VS Code, click Publish Branch or Sync Changes.
crumbs: 4  Working with a remote repository

title: 4  Working with a remote repository
text:
git push

git push -u origin <branch-name>
crumbs: 4  Working with a remote repository

title: 4  Working with a remote repository
section: 4.2 Pull: get the commits of your team mates
text:
4.2 Pull: get the commits of your team mates
git pull
💡 Pull before you start working. Then you always work with the newest version.
crumbs: 4  Working with a remote repository

title: 4  Working with a remote repository
section: 4.3 What happens if your push is rejected?
text:
4.3 What happens if your push is rejected?
If a team mate pushed something since your last pull, GitHub rejects your push:
! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally.
This is not an error in your code. Git just wants you to get the new commits first:

git pull (Git combines their commits with yours).
git push

Usually this works without problems. If you and your team mate changed the same lines of the same file, you get a merge conflict (see chapter 8).
crumbs: 4  Working with a remote repository

title: 4  Working with a remote repository
text:
4.4 Daily workflow
git pull                     # 1. get the newest version
# ... edit your files ...
git status                   # 2. what has changed?
git diff                     # 3. review your changes
git add <file>               # 4. stage
git commit -m "Message"      # 5. commit
git push                     # 6. share
crumbs: 4  Working with a remote repository

title: 5  .gitignore
text:
5.1 You already committed a file by mistake?
Some files should never go into the repository, for example:
Create a file called .gitignore in the main folder of the repository. Write one file name or pattern in each line:
Git ignores these files. They don’t show up in git status anymore.
💡 Use https://www.toptal.com/developers/gitignore to create a .gitignore file for your programming language and IDE.
⚠️ .gitignore only works for files that are not yet committed. Create it at the beginning of the project.
First add the file to .gitignore. Then remove it from the repository, but keep it on your computer:
--cached means: remove it from Git only, not from your disk.
⚠️ The file is still in the old commits. If you committed a password or another secret, removing the file is not enough. Change the password!
Git also ignores empty folders. A folder only appears in the repository when there is at least one file in it.

title: 5  .gitignore
text:
git rm --cached <file>                 # for a file
git rm -r --cached node_modules/       # for a folder
git commit -m "Remove node_modules from repository"

title: 6  Undoing changes
text:
6.1 Look at an old version: detached HEAD
Everybody makes mistakes. Here is how to fix them:
💡 git restore . only resets files that Git already knows. New (untracked) files stay. Use git clean for them.
💡 After git restore --source=..., the old version is in your working directory like a normal change. Commit it if you want to keep it.
⚠️ Only use --amend for commits that you have not pushed yet. For pushed commits, use git revert. It creates a new commit that undoes the old one, so the history of your team mates stays correct.
You can go back in time and look at the whole project as it was in an old commit:
Many tutorials use git checkout <commit-id> for this. It does the same.
Now you are in the detached HEAD state. This means you are not on a branch. git status shows HEAD detached at <commit-id>, and VS Code shows the commit ID instead of a branch name in the bottom left corner.
You can look at the files and run the code, but don’t work here. Commits in this state don’t belong to any branch, and they get lost when you switch away.
Go back to your branch:
💡 Did you make commits in detached HEAD and want to keep them? Create a branch before you switch away: git switch -c <new-branch-name>.

title: 6  Undoing changes
text:
git switch --detach <commit-id>




git switch main

title: 6  Undoing changes
text:
6.2 Put changes aside: stash
Sometimes you have unfinished changes, but you need to pull or switch to another branch. Git may not let you do that. Put your changes aside with:
git stash
Now your working directory is clean. Do what you need to do (e.g. git pull). Then get your changes back:
git stash pop
💡 If your stashed changes and the pulled changes touch the same lines, you get a merge conflict during git stash pop. Solve it like any other conflict (see chapter 8).

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.1 Create a branch
If everybody works directly on main, you constantly get in each other’s way. That’s why each team member works on their own branch:
In the picture, person A and person B both start from the same version of main. Each of them works on their own branch. In the end, both branches are merged, and main contains the work of A and B.
💡 A branch doesn’t prevent merge conflicts. It only moves them to the moment when you merge. The longer a branch lives, the more conflicts you get. So merge often.
First make sure you are on main and have the newest version:
Create a new branch and switch to it:
Choose a name that describes the work, e.g. login-page or 12-fix-menu-crash.
Now edit, stage and commit as usual. Share the branch on GitHub:

title: 7  Branches
7  Branches
text:
7.2 Switch between branches
Show all local branches. The * marks the branch you are on:
git branch
Also show the branches on GitHub (they start with remotes/origin/):
git branch -a
Switch to another branch:
git switch <branch-name>
In VS Code, the name of the current branch is shown in the bottom left corner. Click on it to switch branches.
💡 Commit or stash your changes before you switch branches.

title: 7  Branches
section: 7.3 Keep your branch up to date
text:
7.3 Keep your branch up to date

Reference: https://www.nobledesktop.com/learn/git/git-branches (in this picture, main has its old name master)
While you work on your branch, your team mates merge their work into main. Get their changes into your branch regularly:
git switch main
git pull                     # get the newest main from GitHub
git switch <branch-name>
git merge main               # copy the changes from main into your branch
If there are conflicts, solve them now (see chapter 8). Then push your branch:
git push
It’s better to solve conflicts on your branch than on main.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.4 Merge your branch into main
In a team, we merge branches with a pull request on GitHub (see chapter 9). Then your team can review your work first.
Without a pull request, you can merge on your computer:
git switch main
git pull
git merge <branch-name>
git push
💡 After every merge, test main. Does everything still work?

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.5 Two kinds of merges
When you merge, Git sometimes prints Fast-forward and sometimes creates a new commit. Both are fine.
Fast-forward: main has no new commits since you created your branch. Git simply moves main forward to the newest commit of your branch. No new commit is created.
Merge commit: main and your branch both have new commits. Git combines them in a new merge commit. In git log --oneline --graph you see two lines that join. Git opens your editor for the commit message: check it, save and close it.
💡 On GitHub, the Merge pull request button creates a merge commit by default. So the history always shows which pull request brought in which changes.

title: 7  Branches
text:
7.6 What about rebase?
Maybe you have seen git rebase in a tutorial or on GitHub. It is another way to get the changes from main into your branch:
git switch <branch-name>
git rebase main
Rebase takes your commits and puts them on top of the newest main. The history becomes one straight line, without a merge commit.
In this course we use git merge (see Keep your branch up to date). Merging shows the history as it really happened, and it never changes commits that already exist.
⚠️ Never rebase commits that you have already pushed, or that somebody else has. Rebase throws your old commits away and creates new ones. To push them you would need git push --force, and that deletes the work of your team mates.
💡 Started a rebase and something went wrong? git rebase --abort brings back the state from before.
💡 On GitHub, the Merge button has a dropdown with three options: Create a merge commit (what we use), Squash and merge (all commits of the branch become one) and Rebase and merge (puts the commits on top of main). Use the first one, unless your team agreed on something else.

title: 8  Merge conflicts
text:
8.1 What a conflict looks like
Reference: http://www.cs.utsa.edu/~cs3443/git/merge-conflicts.html
A merge conflict happens when two people change the same lines of the same file. Git can’t decide which version is correct, so you have to decide.
Conflicts can happen during git pull, git merge or git stash pop. Git tells you which files have conflicts:
Git writes both versions into the file and marks them:

title: 8  Merge conflicts
text:
<<<<<<< HEAD
<h1>Welcome to our shop</h1>
=======
<h1>Welcome to the HTL shop</h1>
>>>>>>> main

Between <<<<<<< and =======: your version (VS Code calls it Current Change).
Between ======= and >>>>>>>: the version coming in (VS Code calls it Incoming Change).

title: 8  Merge conflicts
text:
8.2 Solve a conflict

Open the file. VS Code shows buttons above each conflict: Accept Current Change, Accept Incoming Change, Accept Both Changes.
Choose a button, or edit the lines by hand until the code is correct.
Make sure all markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) are gone.
Test your code. Does it still work?
Stage and commit the solved files:

git add <file>
git commit -m "Merge main into login-page"
💡 Talk to your team mate if you are not sure which version is correct.
💡 Want to start over? git merge --abort cancels the merge and brings back the state from before.

title: 9  Pull requests and issues
text:
9.1 Pull requests
A pull request (PR) is a request on GitHub: “Please merge my branch into main.”
Before the merge, your team can:
How to create a pull request:

title: 9  Pull requests and issues
text:
look at all your changes,
write comments and ask questions,
ask you to improve something. You simply commit and push to the same branch, and the pull request updates automatically.



Update your branch with main and push it (see Keep your branch up to date).
Open the repository on GitHub. Click Pull requests → New pull request.
Choose main as base and your branch as compare.
Write a title and a short description of what you did. Click Create pull request.
A team mate reviews the changes and approves them.
Click Merge pull request. Then click Delete branch to remove the branch on GitHub.
On your computer, switch back to main, get the merge and delete your local branch:

git switch main
git pull
git branch -d <branch-name>

title: 9  Pull requests and issues
section: 9.2 Link commits and pull requests to issues
text:
9.2 Link commits and pull requests to issues
In our projects, we plan the work with GitHub issues. Each issue has a number, e.g. #12.
Mention the issue in a commit message. The commit then appears in the history of the issue:
git commit -m "Add input validation to login form #12"
Close the issue automatically with a keyword like closes, fixes or resolves. You can use it in a commit message or in the description of the pull request:
git commit -m "Fix crash when user list is empty, fixes #12"
The issue is closed as soon as the commit or pull request is merged into main.
💡 You can also create a branch directly from an issue: open the issue on GitHub and click Create a branch under Development. GitHub names the branch after the issue, e.g. 12-fix-menu-crash.

title: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control
text:
11.1 Centralized version control (e.g. Subversion)
This chapter is optional. It explains why Git works the way it does.
Reference: https://codentrick.com/architecture-and-design-of-subversion-svn-part-1/
Older tools like Subversion (SVN) use a single central server:
crumbs: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control

title: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control
text:
The history is stored only on the server.
Each developer only has a working copy of the files (svn checkout), without the history.
A commit sends the changes directly to the server. Without a network connection you can’t commit.
crumbs: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control

title: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control
text:
11.2 Distributed version control (Git)

Reference: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/git-features/
With Git, every developer has a complete copy of the repository, including the full history:

You can commit, look at the history and create branches without a network connection.
You decide when to share your commits with git push.
If the server breaks, every clone is a complete backup.
You can push the same repository to several remotes, e.g. GitHub and a school server.
crumbs: 11  Background: centralized vs. distributed version control
